title: install_service() fights the compiler with two lint suppressions instead of cfg-gating the Linux branch
description:
hire/src/main.rs:495-517 — install_service() gates the macOS branch with #[cfg(target_os = "macos")] and ends it with `return Ok(())`, then guards the Linux branch with #[allow(unreachable_code)] because on macOS the compiler correctly sees it as unreachable. That in turn forces #[allow(dead_code)] on LAUNCHD_PLIST at hire/src/main.rs:8 on non-macOS builds.

What goes wrong: two lint suppressions exist purely to paper over a missing cfg, and #[allow(unreachable_code)] on a block is a blunt instrument — it will also silence a genuinely unreachable statement someone adds inside that block later. The `return` in the middle of a function whose other arm falls through is also a re-read: control flow depends on a cfg attribute several lines up.

Rewrite: put the matching negative cfg on the second block and drop everything else.

    #[cfg(target_os = "macos")]
    { ...; println!(...); Ok(()) }

    #[cfg(not(target_os = "macos"))]
    { ...; Ok(()) }

and change hire/src/main.rs:8-9 from #[allow(dead_code)] to #[cfg(target_os = "macos")] on LAUNCHD_PLIST. Same for SYSTEMD_UNIT with #[cfg(not(target_os = "macos"))]. Net effect: two #[allow]s and one `return` deleted, and each platform compiles only its own constant.
